newsitem.title: UK: Long-dated gilts to benefit from UK rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Long-dated gilts to benefit from UK rate rise.

text.p: B Kate Kelland
The long-end of Britain's gilt market should benefit in the long run from a surprise 1/4 point rise in interest rates on Wednesday, analysts said.

The move, bringing the minimum lending rate to 6.0 percent, showed that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke was taking a tough line on inflation and would soothe fears about price pressures emerging further down the line, they said.
"It is a masterful move on the part of the Chancellor," said bond economist Nigel Richardson at Yamaichi International in London. "He has contained inflation pressures well in advance."
December gilt futures initially reacted negatively to the Bank of England's rate move, dipping to 109-24 from 110-00 before the news.
But by 1225 GMT the contract was back up, trading 9/32 higher on the day at 110-02.

"The weight of evidence indicated that, without some rapid monetary tightening, the Chancellor was in danger of both missing his inflation target and losing some hard worn credibility," said Jeremy Peat, chief economist at Royal Bank of Scotland in London.
"This move helps on both counts."
Within Europe, the 10-year gilt yield spread to Bunds remained steady at 169 basis points after the rate hike, showing gilts keeping up pace with a firm German debt market.

Britain has cut official interest rates four times since last December, but recent minutes from meetings between Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George have shown conflict between the two, with George arguing that monetary reins should be tightened.
BoE's George said making a rate move now "to moderate the accelerating pace" of economic growth meant further policy tightenings may be less severe than would otherwise be the case.
Analysts said this, coupled with the market confidence the rate rise would inspire in Clarke's anti-inflation stance, would prove a blessing for 10-year gilt prices and sterling.
Underlying inflation in Britain was at 2.9 percent in September, while gross domestic product data showed a provisional year-on-year rise of 2.3 percent in Q3 1996.
"This will be seen as a positive move by the Chancellor. It's positive for the pound and positive for the gilt market too," said Rob Hayward, economist at BankAmerica in London.
But he said there may be some short-term market doubts about what the rate hike would mean for the November budget.
Clarke is due to deliver Britain's budget on November 26 -- the last before a general election must be called by May 1997.
Fears that the government may push the Chancellor to include sizeable, vote-winning tax cuts in the package -- risking a stoke-up in inflation -- had been worrying gilt investors, analysts said.
But Yamaichi's Richardson said the 1/4 point rate rise would help allay some concerns about looser fiscal policy.
"The Chancellor can now not be accused of being overtly political in the budget," Richardson said. "The rate rise has opened the way to tax cuts."
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
